name: Google Effect
description: When people expect information to stay easily searchable online, they tend to remember the information itself less and remember the route back to it more. The mind offloads content memory toward location or access memory when retrieval feels cheap.
design_relevance_note: Directly relevant to search, knowledge management, note-taking, bookmarks, AI assistants, reminders, and saved-state features. Products can change whether users memorize content, memorize retrieval paths, or rely on the system entirely.
prevalence_note: Recognizable in search, note-taking, knowledge-management, and AI-assistant conversations, but still not a routinely cited named heuristic across mainstream day-to-day product design.

findings.description: A meta-analysis found the Google Effect on memory is closely associated with cognitive load, behavioral phenotype, and cognitive self-esteem, and is stronger on mobile devices than computers. People with a larger existing knowledge base are less susceptible; the effect is stronger for those with prior internet-use experience; and North American participants showed greater susceptibility than other regions. Real, design-relevant moderators (device type, user's existing knowledge, prior tech experience) beyond a simple universal effect.
findings.source_title: Google effects on memory: a meta-analytical review of the media effects of intensive Internet search behavior

findings.description: Across four experiments, expecting information to remain accessible later reduced recall for the information itself and improved memory for where it could be found, consistent with the Internet functioning as a form of external or transactive memory.
findings.source_title: Google Effects on Memory: Cognitive Consequences of Having Information at Our Fingertips
